ideas.hypothesis: Long periods of low mortgage rates push house prices up faster than they lower repayment burdens for low-income young households. As a result, low-rate periods raise the chance that bottom-income-quintile households stay long-term renters, while they speed up renter-to-owner moves for top-quintile households.
ideas.test: Use an Australian household panel (e.g., HILDA 2001-2019) of tenure transitions merged with the standard variable mortgage rate. Estimate a discrete-time hazard of renter-to-owner transition with interactions of rate level x income quintile x age group, controlling for local house prices.
ideas.disconfirming: Low rates raise renter-to-owner transitions equally or more for low-income households than for high-income households.

ideas.hypothesis: Adopting a formal inflation target lowers the probability that the short-term rate is in the high-volatility regime and makes the low-volatility regime more persistent, with the regime transition probabilities shifting at the adoption date.
ideas.test: Estimate a two-regime diffusion model of weekly 3-month bill rates for Canada, New Zealand, the UK and Sweden, with an inflation-targeting adoption dummy in the time-varying transition equation. Use non-adopting countries over the same years as placebos.
ideas.disconfirming: The adoption dummy has no effect on transition probabilities, or the post-adoption share of time in the high-volatility regime is no lower than in non-adopters.

ideas.hypothesis: Pass-through of negative policy rates to retail term-deposit rates is cut off near zero, and the cut-off is sharper for banks that rely more on household deposits. So the deposit-rate pass-through coefficient drops markedly once the policy rate goes below zero.
ideas.test: Use a bank-level monthly panel of term-deposit rates in the euro area, Sweden and Denmark for 2010-2019. Run a piecewise (kinked) pass-through regression with the kink at a zero policy rate, interacted with each bank's household deposit funding share.
ideas.disconfirming: The pass-through coefficient below zero is statistically the same as above zero, or does not vary with deposit funding share.

ideas.hypothesis: For life insurers holding interest-indexed annuities, negative rates widen the duration gap: crediting-rate floors make surrender behaviour less sensitive to rates, which raises the loss in economic value per basis-point move.
ideas.test: Calibrate the logit surrender model to European annuity data and compute liability duration and convexity under positive and negative rate scenarios. Then compare listed insurers' equity sensitivity to rate shocks before and after 2014 in negative-rate countries versus other countries.
ideas.disconfirming: Duration gaps and the equity sensitivity of insurers to rates do not change when rates turn negative.

ideas.hypothesis: Mortgage rate increases cut purchases by first-time buyers more than purchases by repeat buyers, because first-time buyers sit closer to the payment-to-income affordability constraint captured by an affordable-price measure.
ideas.test: Use metro-level mortgage origination data with first-time buyer flags (e.g., UK product sales data or US agency loan data). Regress purchase counts on mortgage rate changes, interacted with buyer type and the metro's initial gap between affordable and actual price.
ideas.disconfirming: First-time buyer purchase elasticities to rate increases are equal to or smaller than those of repeat buyers.

ideas.hypothesis: Economies further along the demographic transition (lower fertility and mortality, higher old-age dependency) have lower long-run real interest rates, and the timing of the long decline in Belgian real rates follows the phases of its demographic transition.
ideas.test: Build a long historical panel for Belgium and neighbouring countries (1850-2019) of government bond yields, inflation, birth and death rates and dependency ratios. Estimate panel cointegration regressions of real rates on demographic variables.
ideas.disconfirming: There is no relationship, or a positive one, between the stage of the demographic transition and real interest rates.

ideas.hypothesis: Structural breaks in the natural rate of interest appear first in long forward rates. Long-horizon forwards adjust to breaks in real-time natural-rate estimates within a few quarters, while short rates lag because of policy-rule inertia.
ideas.test: Date breakpoints (e.g., Bai-Perron) in real-time vintages of natural-rate estimates and in US 5-year-5-year forward rates and short rates for 1985-2019, then compare break dates and adjustment speeds.
ideas.disconfirming: Breaks in forward rates do not line up with natural-rate breaks, or they lag the breaks in short rates.

ideas.hypothesis: Under adaptive learning, the inflation target band that bond markets perceive gets narrower and more symmetric with time since the target was announced, so the asymmetry found for Canada fades in later subsamples.
ideas.test: Re-estimate the target-zone term-structure model on rolling windows of Canadian yields and inflation for 1991-2019, and repeat for New Zealand and the UK. Track the perceived band width and its asymmetry over time.
ideas.disconfirming: The perceived band width and asymmetry stay constant or grow with time since the announcement.

ideas.hypothesis: Nominal mortgage payments front-load real repayments (the tilt effect), so a rise in long-run inflation expectations lowers measured affordability and nominal house prices even when real rates are unchanged.
ideas.test: Use a metro panel of house prices, median income and mortgage rates. Split the mortgage rate into a real component and an expected-inflation component (from breakevens or surveys), then compare their coefficients in the intrinsic-value house price model.
ideas.disconfirming: The expected-inflation component has no effect on affordability or prices once the real rate is controlled for.

ideas.hypothesis: Long periods of low interest rates raise the premiums health insurers file, because lower investment income on reserves has to be made up in pricing. The effect is larger for insurers whose reserves have longer duration.
ideas.test: Merge insurer-level marketplace premium rate filings for 2014-2019 with statutory statements on portfolio yields and reserve duration. Regress premium growth on portfolio yield, interacted with reserve duration, with state-year fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Portfolio yields have no association with premium growth, or the association does not vary with reserve duration.

ideas.hypothesis: Small open economies whose policy rule includes an exchange-rate stabilization term spend more time in the high-volatility regime of the short rate, because the interest rate absorbs currency shocks; in exchange they have lower exchange-rate volatility.
ideas.test: Estimate regime-switching diffusions of short rates for managed-exchange-rate economies (e.g., Denmark) and free floaters (e.g., Sweden, Norway) for 1995-2019, and compare regime durations and the high-volatility share.
ideas.disconfirming: Managed-exchange-rate economies do not spend more time in the high-volatility regime than floaters.

ideas.hypothesis: Microfinance lending rates respond weakly and with long lags to central bank policy rate changes, because operating costs rather than funding costs dominate their pricing. Their pass-through is lower than that of commercial bank lending rates in the same country.
ideas.test: Use an institution-level panel of microfinance yields on loan portfolios (e.g., from a global microfinance database) for countries with policy-rate series. Estimate error-correction pass-through models and compare them with commercial bank lending-rate pass-through.
ideas.disconfirming: Microfinance pass-through is as large and as fast as commercial bank pass-through.

ideas.hypothesis: Higher personal income tax rates on interest income make household term-deposit volumes less responsive to nominal deposit rates, and after-tax deposit rates explain deposit growth better than pre-tax rates.
ideas.test: Use a quarterly panel for Latvia, Estonia, Sweden, Finland and Denmark (2000-2019) of household deposit volumes, deposit rates and statutory tax rates on interest income. Exploit changes in tax rates and compare models using pre-tax and after-tax rates.
ideas.disconfirming: Pre-tax rates fit deposit growth as well as after-tax rates, and changes in interest-income tax do not shift deposit responsiveness.

ideas.hypothesis: Higher effective local property tax rates dampen the sensitivity of nominal house prices to nominal interest rates, because tax capitalization shares the affordability burden. An intrinsic-value model that includes property taxes fits better.
ideas.test: Use a metro panel of house prices, incomes and mortgage rates with effective property tax rates. Add a nominal rate x property tax interaction to the intrinsic-value model and compare out-of-sample fit.
ideas.disconfirming: The interaction term is zero or positive (it amplifies rate sensitivity), and adding property taxes does not improve fit.

ideas.hypothesis: Near the zero lower bound, interest-indexed annuity liabilities show more negative convexity, because surrender options sit asymmetrically in or out of the money. This raises insurers' hedging demand for long bonds.
ideas.test: Simulate annuity value, duration and convexity with the logit surrender model at starting rate levels from 5% down to 0%. Empirically, regress insurers' net purchases of long bonds on how close the policy rate is to zero, using regulatory holdings data.
ideas.disconfirming: Liability convexity does not change with rate level, or insurer long-bond demand does not rise near the zero lower bound.

ideas.hypothesis: Interest rate increases lower credit scores more for young, high debt-to-income borrowers who hold variable-rate debt, through more missed payments.
ideas.test: Run an event study on an anonymized credit bureau panel around the 2004-2006 and 2015-2018 tightening cycles, splitting borrowers by age, debt-to-income ratio and share of variable-rate debt.
ideas.disconfirming: Score changes after rate increases do not differ by debt-to-income ratio, age or variable-rate exposure.

ideas.hypothesis: A flatter or inverted yield curve predicts higher metro house price volatility in the following quarters, especially in metros with a high share of adjustable-rate mortgages.
ideas.test: Use quarterly metro house price indices for 1990-2019. Estimate conditional volatility (GARCH or regime-switching), then regress it on the lagged term spread interacted with metro adjustable-rate mortgage share.
ideas.disconfirming: The term spread has no predictive power for house price volatility, including in high adjustable-rate metros.

ideas.hypothesis: After the South African Reserve Bank adopted inflation targeting in 2000, the short rate moved into a persistent lower-volatility regime, with the 2008 crisis causing only a temporary high-volatility spell.
ideas.test: Estimate a regime-switching diffusion with time-varying transition probabilities on weekly South African 3-month Treasury bill rates for 1990-2019, with a post-2000 shifter in the transition equation.
ideas.disconfirming: Regime probabilities and persistence show no shift after 2000.

ideas.hypothesis: Low mortgage rates raise purchasing power most for larger suburban homes, so people who buy in low-rate periods end up with longer commutes than buyers in high-rate periods.
ideas.test: Use national household travel or community survey microdata on owner-occupiers, with year moved in and commute time and distance. Regress commute length on the mortgage rate in the purchase year, controlling for metro, income and household type.
ideas.disconfirming: Commute length of recent buyers is unrelated to, or falls with, lower mortgage rates at purchase.

ideas.hypothesis: After interest rate increases, build-out in greenfield new housing developments slows more than infill construction, because buyers in such estates are mostly first-home builders who depend on construction and land loans.
ideas.test: Use estate-level lot settlement and building approval data for Melbourne growth-corridor developments (2005-2019) against cash rate changes, and compare with established-area approvals using local projections.
ideas.disconfirming: Greenfield estates are no more rate-sensitive than infill development.

ideas.hypothesis: Transit-oriented development projects have high upfront capital costs and long paybacks, so they are more sensitive to long-term rates: permits on transit-station parcels fall more than conventional permits after rises in 10-year yields.
ideas.test: Use parcel-level building permits within half a mile of rail stations versus elsewhere in several US metros (2000-2019), and regress permit counts on 10-year yield changes interacted with station proximity.
ideas.disconfirming: Permits near stations respond to long rates no more than permits elsewhere.

ideas.hypothesis: Mortgage rate increases delay first births among renters who plan to buy and among recent buyers with high payment-to-income ratios, linking monetary tightening to fertility timing through housing costs.
ideas.test: Use a household panel (e.g., HILDA) linking first-birth hazards to mortgage rate changes. Use a difference-in-differences comparing variable-rate with fixed-rate mortgagors, and renters by stated intention to buy.
ideas.disconfirming: Birth hazards of variable-rate mortgagors and would-be buyers do not change after rate increases relative to the comparison groups.

ideas.hypothesis: Negative policy rates are not passed through to consumer credit rates; banks widen consumer credit spreads to protect margins squeezed on deposits, so consumer borrowing does not expand.
ideas.test: Run a difference-in-differences on bank-level consumer credit rates and volumes in euro area, Danish and Swedish banks versus non-negative-rate countries around 2014-2015, using harmonized interest-rate statistics.
ideas.disconfirming: Consumer credit rates fall roughly one-for-one with the policy rate below zero and volumes rise.

ideas.hypothesis: The two-regime result for the short rate (volatility, not drift, differs across regimes) replicates on post-2008 US data and on other countries, but time-varying transition probabilities lose explanatory power at the zero lower bound.
ideas.test: Re-estimate the same specification on weekly 3-month bill rates for the US (2009-2019) and for Canada, the UK and Germany. Compare parameter estimates and likelihood-ratio tests of the regime and transition-variable restrictions.
ideas.disconfirming: Two distinct volatility regimes are not identified in the new samples, or drift rather than volatility separates the regimes.

ideas.hypothesis: Interest rates on agricultural operating loans vary with the seasons, following planting and harvest cycles: farms borrowing at peak season pay higher rates, especially from non-bank lenders.
ideas.test: Use quarterly agricultural loan rate surveys and farm-level loan records from a national farm finance survey (ARMS). Regress loan rates on month or quarter-of-origination dummies, with lender-type interactions and controls for farm type.
ideas.disconfirming: Origination-season dummies are jointly insignificant for loan rates.

ideas.hypothesis: Indian retail term-deposit rates track the Taylor-rule implied policy rate more closely than the actual policy rate, suggesting that banks price the expected policy path into deposits.
ideas.test: Estimate a Taylor rule on Indian monthly data (2000-2019) to get implied rates, then regress term-deposit rates on both the actual and the implied policy rates in a horse-race specification.
ideas.disconfirming: The actual policy rate dominates, and the implied rate adds no explanatory power.

ideas.hypothesis: Policy rate hikes raise rents in tight rental markets with a one-to-two-year lag, because they hold back renter-to-owner transitions and the financing of new rental supply.
ideas.test: Run local projections of metro rent indices on identified monetary policy shocks (e.g., high-frequency surprises) for 2000-2019, with interactions for initial rental vacancy rates.
ideas.disconfirming: Rents fall or do not respond to tightening shocks, even in low-vacancy markets.

ideas.hypothesis: Farms adopt capital-embodied technologies (e.g., precision agriculture equipment) faster in low-rate periods, and the effect is stronger for highly leveraged, credit-dependent farms.
ideas.test: Use repeated farm survey waves (ARMS) with technology adoption modules, merged with farm loan rates. Run probit regressions of adoption on rate level x debt-to-asset ratio, controlling for farm type and region.
ideas.disconfirming: Adoption is unrelated to rate levels or does not vary with leverage.

ideas.hypothesis: Increases in auto loan rates reduce car purchases among young households and shift them toward walking and public transport, more so in mixed-use, New Urbanist-style neighbourhoods where alternatives exist.
ideas.test: Use national household travel survey waves merged with auto loan rates at the survey date. Model vehicle ownership and mode share of young households on rates, interacted with neighbourhood density and land-use mix.
ideas.disconfirming: Vehicle ownership and car mode share do not respond to auto loan rates, in any neighbourhood type.

ideas.hypothesis: In more competitive bank deposit markets, deposit rates beat annuity crediting rates more often, which raises annuity surrender rates and the asset-liability duration risk insurers carry.
ideas.test: Use an insurer-by-region panel of annuity surrender rates linked to local deposit-market concentration (HHI) and the deposit-minus-crediting-rate spread, estimated with the logit surrender specification.
ideas.disconfirming: Local bank competition has no association with surrender rates once the rate spread is controlled for, and it does not amplify the spread effect.
